title: Neti, neti: not this, not this
hookLine: Yajnavalkya tells a king who the true self is by saying what it isn't
carry: neti neti: the self is beyond every name
tomorrow: the peace chant — purnam adah, purnam idam — from fullness, fullness
last: KRATU — AS IS HIS DESIRE, SO IS HIS WILL.

cards: Neti, neti. Not this, not this. One word, said twice: a description that works by refusing to describe.
It's been woven through the book. It's in the chapter where Shakalya lost his head. It's much earlier, too, in book two.
And it comes back at the high point of Yajnavalkya's talk with King Janaka, later in the same talk as the snake's old skin, when he's ready to say who the self really is.

teach.b: He is the great unborn self, Yajnavalkya says, the one made of knowing among the senses. He lies in the space within the heart, ruler of all, lord of all. He doesn't grow greater by good deeds, or smaller by bad ones.
People seek him through study, through ritual, through giving, through fasting. Knowing him, one becomes a sage. Longing for him, wanderers leave home.
And then: sa esha neti neti atma. That self is not this, not this. He can't be grasped, for he is never grasped.
He can't be destroyed, for he is never destroyed. He doesn't cling, for he never clings.
He is unbound; he doesn't tremble; he isn't harmed.
In book two the text had already said why this is the highest teaching: there is nothing higher than this not. That's the atman, the true self this whole book has been hunting for. Here's the logic.
Everything you can name is something seen, and Ushasta learned you can't see the seer. So every name falls short. Not the body.
Not the breath. Not the mind. Not the dream, not even deep sleep.
Each not clears a little more room. Hindu schools hear these two words differently. Shankara, in Advaita, hears them refusing every description, because Brahman is beyond all qualities.

teach.h: BEYOND ALL QUALITIES, OR NOT ONLY THIS?
teach.b: Ramanuja hears them saying not only this: Brahman isn't limited to anything just described, because its good qualities have no end. Both take the words seriously.
And in book four, after the book tells the whole Maitreyi conversation one more time, it says simply: having said this, Yajnavalkya went away. The man who left finally leaves.

how: Neti neti is used as a method of inquiry in Advaita Vedanta, where students set aside body, breath and mind as not the self; other Vedanta schools read the phrase as denying any limit to Brahman.

o: an order to give up the body, breath and mind
a name for the great unborn self in the heart
not so, not this: describing the self by refusing

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.
p: na iti: not so, not this
lies in the space within the heart
not only this: its goodness has no end

s: neti neti appears only once in the Brihadaranyaka
it comes back several times: in book two, in Shakalya's chapter, and here.
the text says the self grows greater by good deeds
he grows neither greater by good deeds nor smaller by bad ones.
the book says Yajnavalkya finally went away
after telling the Maitreyi conversation again: having said this, he went away.

games.q: Priya's list: debate kid, dancer, a bad grade this week. by neti neti, which one is her self?
o: the dancer, since she loves it most.
none of them: each is real, but the self is the one who knows them all.
the bad grade, since that's what's true right now.
games.why: not this, not this. the labels aren't thrown away; they just aren't the atman, which is never grasped and never harmed.

practice: Let the labels you use for yourself come up one at a time: a name, a job, a role in a family, a mood from today.
Give each one a breath, and as it goes out, say inwardly: not this, not to throw it away, since each one is real, but because in the text's terms it isn't the self.
Then rest with the text's last words: unbound, unharmed, not trembling.

wordCard.voice: Neti. Na iti: not so, not this. In the Brihadaranyaka, said twice, the way the self is described by refusing every description.

orig.note: Sanskrit na (not) + iti (thus): not so, not this. sa eṣa neti nety ātmā.

carryVoice: Your line: neti neti, the self is beyond every name. Tomorrow, the chant that closes the book. That's day three hundred eighty-seven.
